newsitem.title: MEXICO: Carso's Slim strikes again - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Carso's Slim strikes again - analysts.

text.p: Mexican holding company Grupo Carso SA's takeover of Sears Roebuck and Co's troubled Mexican unit is a textbook move for Carso's billionaire owner Carlos Slim: buy it cheap and try and turn it around.

Carso said on Wednesday it will pay about $103 million for 60 percent of Sears de Mexico SA and will buy another 25 percent stake from the public for some $42 million. Sears Roebuck will retain a 15 percent stake in the Mexican firm.
"It is a classic move by Slim. They have always been shrewd buyers and they never pay too much for what they buy," Daniel Goldstein, an analyst at ING Barings in Mexico City, told Reuters.

During this decade, Carso has grown by leaps and bounds, transforming itself from a small real estate, retail and tire company to Mexico's biggest conglomerate with interests in everything from telecommunications to cigarrettes.
At every step, the company has grown in the same way: buying troubled firms cheaply and making them efficient and profitable.
This time around, Carso has not gobbled up a large company, but analysts said it again appears to have paid a good price, even including some $184 million it will likely take on in Sears' debt.

Sears said Carso paid a 40 percent premium over the recent market price of Sears de Mexico's shares. But analysts estimated Carso paid about half of Sears de Mexico's book value and about a third of its yearly sales.
"They bought a top shelf name that had been underperforming for years," said Bear Stearns' Carso analyst Santiago Pique.

Sears de Mexico was ripe for a takeover, having racked up eight consecutive quarters of operating losses. In 1996, Sears de Mexico lost 190.65 million pesos, but its operating losses were 449.18 million pesos.
Part of the problem for Sears was sluggish sales in the wake of the 1994-1995 peso crash, but the company was also seen as suffering from a bad image and poor positioning.
"Even before the devaluation, Sears had trouble at the merchandising level," said Christine Aimar, a retail analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in Mexico City.
By buying Sears a few months ahead of what is expected to be a consumer-led economic rebound, Carso could simply watch the retailer ride a growing wave of consumer spending.
But it is likely Carso will tighten the belt at the retailer, slashing costs and laying off workers, analysts said.

"Slim can turn it around. It can't get much worse. But whether he can turn it into a highly profitable business with synergies, I don't know," said Sebastian Barry Taylor, a retail analyst at ING Barings.
The effect on Carso's income statement will not be large, analysts said. Sears will probably add about 8-10 percent to Carso's revenues, but will cut between 3-5 percent off its operating profits.
Carso will likely leverage the buy and will not likely make any other major acquisitions in the short-term, analysts said.
